title: The Four-Minute Mile with Pacers
text:
By 1954 the four-minute mile had become a famous barrier. Gunder Haegg of Sweden had run 4:01.4 in 1945, and nobody had gone faster since. Roger Bannister, a British medical student who trained in short sessions around his hospital work, believed it could be done, but not alone.

He planned the attempt with two friends and fellow runners, Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway, with advice from the coach Franz Stampfl. The idea was simple: Brasher would set the pace for the first two laps, Chataway would take over for the third, and Bannister would save himself for the final lap, running at even speed without having to think about the clock.

On 6 May 1954, at the Iffley Road track in Oxford, the wind was gusting so strongly that Bannister almost called it off. Minutes before the start it eased, and the three decided to go. Brasher led through two laps, with Bannister at one point shouting at him to go faster and Brasher ignoring him, sticking to the plan. Chataway took over and led through the bell. With about 300 yards left Bannister passed him and drove for the line, collapsing as he crossed it.

The announcer, Norris McWhirter, began reading out the time, and after the word "three" the rest was lost in the crowd's roar: 3:59.4. Bannister later stressed that the record had been a shared effort. About seven weeks later John Landy of Australia ran faster still.
lesson: Even a solo achievement often rests on a team. Ask for help with the parts others can carry, and trust the plan you made together when the moment gets hard.
people: Roger Bannister, Chris Brasher, Chris Chataway, Franz Stampfl
location: Iffley Road track, Oxford, United Kingdom
